title: Church Hurt as Institutional Formation: Governance, Conditional Belonging, and Religious Harm Among Black Millennials and Generation Z
content: This article theorizes spiritual harm in Black Church spaces as institutional governance formation—a structurally embedded set of organizational practices through which sacred institutions regulate identity, discipline desire, and secure communal coherence through the conditional extension and withdrawal of belonging. Drawing on the religious harm and spiritual abuse literature and on organizational sociology, the article argues that harm within the Black Church is neither individual incident nor clinical event but organizational reproduction: transmitted through institutional grammar, stabilized across generations, and legible in the gap between members’ relationship to Christianity as a theological tradition and their relationship to the Black Church as an institution. The analysis integrates a concurrent embedded mixed-methods study of African American Millennials and Generation Z (N = 173 survey respondents; 8 semi-structured interviews; digital ethnography), in which qualitative data carry primary evidential weight, with national survey data from the Pew Research Center and PRRI that contextualize the study’s mechanism-level findings at population scale. The article foregrounds the depth and irreplaceability of Black congregational belonging—documented at national scale—as the structural precondition that makes conditional belonging effective as a governance instrument. It closes by reframing generational disaffiliation not as secular drift but as an institutional legitimacy signal produced by the widening gap between the Black Church’s founding promise and its governance practice.
